## One science observation {.smaller}

A single spectrum from MAVEN's ultraviolet spectrograph (IUVS), time-tagged by the spacecraft clock.

To turn it into science, someone has to answer:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **When** was it taken, in a standard time system (UTC, TAI, TDB, ...)?
- **Where** was MAVEN?
- **Which way** was it pointing?
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **What** did the slit see: limb, disk, sky?
- **What** was the viewing geometry? Solar zenith, emission, phase, and ray nadir angles; local time
- **How far** was the light from the target?
:::
::::

. . .

::: {.callout}
None of these are answered by the instrument telemetry. They can be answered using **ancillary data products**, each of which comes from a different team.
:::

::: notes
Start from a measurement everyone in the data systems group has handled. The point: the science file is only useful once it is joined with geometry, and that geometry is somebody else's product.
:::

## Who knows what

| Question | Who knows | Cadence | SPICE kernel |
|---|---|---|---|
| UTC ↔ uniform time | IERS (leap seconds) | rarely | **LSK** |
| Clock count ↔ time | mission ops, time correlation | days/weeks | **SCLK** |
| Where is the s/c? | navigation (JPL NAV for MAVEN) | days | **SPK** |
| Where are the planets? | JPL Solar System Dynamics | years | **SPK** |
| Which way is the s/c oriented? | attitude telemetry (spacecraft ops) | daily | **CK** |
| How are instruments mounted? | spacecraft builder, instrument team | rarely | **FK**, **IK** |
| Shape and orientation of the target | IAU, science teams | rarely | **PCK**, **DSK** |

::: {.small .muted}
Different owners, different update rates, different sizes, different formats. SPICE's whole design follows from this table.
:::

::: notes
Ask the room who on the team has touched each of these, even indirectly. Most will say "time_convert" or "some geometry library" without knowing which kernels sat behind it.
:::

## SPICE's design answer

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 9
%%| fig-height: 3
flowchart LR
  NAV[Navigation] --> SPK[(SPK)]
  OPS[Spacecraft ops] --> CK[(CK)]
  TC[Time correlation] --> SCLK[(SCLK)]
  INST[Instrument team] --> IK[(FK / IK)]
  IERS[IERS / IAU] --> LSK[(LSK / PCK)]
  SPK & CK & SCLK & IK & LSK --> POOL{{"kernel pool<br/>(in your process)"}}
  POOL --> API["spice function"]
  API --> YOU[Your code]
```

::: {.small}
Each kind of ancillary data lives in **its own file type**, produced and versioned by whoever owns it. The **SPICE toolkit** combines them only at query time.
:::

## Why one answer needs 6–10 files

"Where did the IUVS boresight hit Mars at this clock tick, and was it illuminated?"

| Step | Kernel |
|---|---|
| clock tick → ET | **SCLK** + **LSK** |
| MAVEN relative to Mars | **SPK** (MAVEN) + **SPK** (planets) |
| spacecraft attitude | **CK** (indexed by SCLK) |
| boresight in spacecraft frame | **FK** + **IK** |
| Mars shape and orientation | **PCK** (or **DSK**) |

::: {.small .muted}
Miss any one and the call fails, loudly. That is a feature: SPICE errors name the missing piece.
:::

## A developer's model

Think of SPICE the way you'd think of a database:

- **Kernels are a read-only data store.** Loading files with `furnsh` is like attaching data sources.
- **Each API call is a query.** `str2et` and `spkpos` ask a question; SPICE finds the answer in whatever is loaded.
- **The caller never names a file.** The **kernel pool** decides which file answers.

```python
import spiceypy as sp

sp.furnsh("session01.tm")                          # load a list of kernels

et = sp.str2et("2026-11-19T12:00:00")               # query 1: time   (LSK)
pos, lt = sp.spkpos("MOON", et, "J2000",            # query 2: state  (SPK)
                    "NONE", "EARTH")
```

## The kernel pool is global state

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**What that means**

- One pool per process; every function sees it.
- `kclear()` empties it for everyone.
- Data loaded **later** win when two kernels cover the same thing.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Why developers care**

- Load once, at startup, in one place.
- CSPICE is **not thread-safe**: one SPICE caller per process, or a lock.
- Log what you loaded (`ktotal` / `kdata`). It's an upper bound on what was used, so load as little as you need.
- Kernels must be on a **local (POSIX) file system**.
:::
::::

::: notes
This is the slide most relevant to the data systems group. Long-running services, Dask workers and multiprocessing pools all trip over the global pool. Keep the deeper discussion for the discussion block.
:::

## Two kinds of files

| | Text kernels | Binary kernels |
|---|---|---|
| Types | LSK, SCLK, PCK (text), FK, IK, meta-kernel | SPK, CK, PCK (binary), DSK |
| Format | `KEY = value` assignments in `\begindata` blocks | DAF/DAS arrays with a comment area |
| Size | kilobytes | megabytes to gigabytes |
| Edited by | people, in an editor | programs (`mkspk`, `msopck`, `spkw*`) |
| Why | constants humans review and diff | dense time series searched fast |

::: {.small .muted}
Text kernels can be read and diffed like code. Binary kernels can't: inspect them with toolkit utilities (`brief`, `ckbrief`, `commnt`) or API calls, never a text editor.
:::

## Meta-kernels: convenient, but not provenance {.smaller}

```{.text}
KPL/MK
\begindata
   PATH_VALUES     = ( '../kernels' )
   PATH_SYMBOLS    = ( 'KERNELS' )
   KERNELS_TO_LOAD = ( '$KERNELS/naif0012.tls'
                       '$KERNELS/pck00011.tpc'
                       '$KERNELS/de440s.bsp' )
\begintext
```

- One `furnsh` loads them all, **in this order**: later files have priority.
- **Fragile paths.** Relative paths resolve against the *working directory*, not the `.tm` file, so a meta-kernel that works on one machine often breaks on another.
- **Loaded ≠ used.** A mission-wide meta-kernel loads everything for the whole mission. It records what was *available*, not the minimum set SPICE actually used for your answer.

::: {.callout}
**Opinion: **
Don't load a mission-wide meta-kernel blindly. For provenance, record the **minimum set of kernels covering your time range**. LASP projects such as **EMM** and **IMAP** keep a kernel database and utilities that return exactly that set.
:::

::: notes
Presenter's opinion, stated as such: meta-kernels are handy for notebooks and quick scripts, but in production pipelines they are fragile and say little about provenance. EMM and IMAP have built kernel databases (possibly other LASP projects too); invite people from those teams to say how theirs work.
:::

## Kernels document themselves {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Comment area of `de440s.bsp` (excerpt)

```{.text}
JPL planetary and lunar ephemeris DE440
Integrated 25 June 2020
Reference: R.S. Park et al., Astronomical Journal,
  DOI: 10.3847/1538-3881/abd414
...
Time span covered by ephemeris:
26-DEC-1849 00:00 to   22-JAN-2150 00:00

Bodies included:
  MERCURY BARYCENTER (1)  SATURN BARYCENTER (6)  MERCURY (199)
  VENUS BARYCENTER (2)    URANUS BARYCENTER (7)  VENUS (299)
  EARTH BARYCENTER (3)    NEPTUNE BARYCENTER (8) MOON (301)
  MARS BARYCENTER (4)     PLUTO BARYCENTER (9)   EARTH (399)
  JUPITER BARYCENTER (5)  SUN (10)
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Comments answer the questions you'd otherwise email someone about:** who made the file, from what data, the time span it covers, what's in it (and what isn't), and known problems.

- Text kernels: open in an editor.
- Binary kernels: `commnt -r file.bsp`.

**Start with the `aareadme.txt`.** Many NAIF kernel directories have one, e.g. [`generic_kernels/`](https://naif.jpl.nasa.gov/pub/naif/generic_kernels/){target="_blank" preview-link="false"}, [`generic_kernels/pck/`](https://naif.jpl.nasa.gov/pub/naif/generic_kernels/pck/){target="_blank" preview-link="false"} and [`MAVEN/kernels/`](https://naif.jpl.nasa.gov/pub/naif/MAVEN/kernels/){target="_blank" preview-link="false"}. It explains naming, versions, and which file to use.
:::
::::

::: notes
Point at the body list: Mars barycenter (4) is there, Mars itself (499) is not. The comments told you that before any code failed. That is the hook for the barycenter discussion in Session 3. In spk/planets the readme files are named aareadme_de430-de431.txt and aa_summaries.txt, so "aa*" is the pattern to look for.
:::
